title: The Fifth and Sixth Centuries
orientation: Russell surveys the fifth century's barbarian invasions and the collapse of the Western Empire, the fierce Christological controversies between Nestorius and Cyril that convulsed the Church, and then turns to the sixth century's Boethius -- whose Consolation of Philosophy, written in a Gothic prison awaiting execution, Russell treats as an extraordinary island of calm, Platonic rationalism in an otherwise superstitious and dogma-obsessed age. The chapter matters as a bridge: it shows almost no original philosophy being produced for a century, and then, in Boethius, a solitary transmitter who carried Platonic philosophy into the medieval world under a guise the Church could accept as orthodox.
historical_background: The fifth century saw the Gothic sack of Rome (410) and, in 476, the end of the Western Roman Empire when Odovaker deposed the last emperor; the Huns under Attila invaded Gaul in 451 and were defeated at Chalons, then turned on Italy before Attila's death. Germanic kingdoms replaced centralized Roman administration across Western Europe: the Angles and Saxons invaded Britain, the Franks took Gaul, the Vandals took Spain and then Africa, and the Visigoths settled in southern France. In the sixth century, Theodoric the Ostrogoth ruled Italy while preserving Roman law and administration, until his execution of his minister Boethius in 524; the Emperor Justinian (527-565) then attempted to reconquer the West, ruinously prolonging war in Italy, closed the pagan schools of philosophy at Athens in 529, and built the church of St. Sophia.
philosophical_problems: How should the relationship between Christ's divine and human natures be understood -- as two persons, one nature, or two natures in one person?
Is evil a positive thing, or merely a privation (an absence) of good, given that an omnipotent, wholly good God can do everything?
What is the relationship between happiness (blessedness) and the good, and between the good and God?
Can a life of pure philosophical calm and virtue be achieved independently of Christian dogma, sin-obsession, and superstition?

philosophers_discussed.name: Boethius
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's primary philosophical subject: a Roman senator executed by Theodoric in 524, whose Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison, Russell treats as purely Platonic in content though later read throughout the Middle Ages as an orthodox Christian work, and praises as a singular achievement of calm, rational philosophy unmatched, in Russell's judgment, until after Newton.

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Cyril of Alexandria
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Patriarch of Alexandria and 'advocate of unity' of Christ's nature against Nestorius; described by Russell, quoting Gibbon, as a fanatic who incited pogroms against Alexandria's Jews and whose followers lynched the Neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia; presided, by force of arrival first, over the Council of Ephesus (431) that condemned Nestorius.

philosophers_discussed.name: Nestorius
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Patriarch of Constantinople who held that Christ's human and divine natures constituted two distinct Persons, and objected on this ground to calling the Virgin 'Mother of God'; condemned as a heretic at the Council of Ephesus (431), founding the Nestorian sect that spread through Syria, Persia, India, and eventually China.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named by Boethius, along with Socrates and Aristotle, as one of the 'true philosophers,' as against the Stoics and Epicureans, whom Boethius regards as usurpers of philosophy's name; the Consolation is described by Russell as purely Platonic in its metaphysics.

philosophers_discussed.name: Justinian
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Emperor from 527 to 565, chiefly noted for his Digest of Roman law, his closing of the pagan philosophical schools at Athens in 529, his building of St. Sophia, and his costly, only partially successful attempt to reconquer Italy and Africa from the Goths and Vandals.

philosophers_discussed.name: Theodoric
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Ostrogothic King of Italy (493-526) who, though an Arian, preserved Roman civil administration, law, and the Senate, and was on good terms with the Catholic Church until his last years, when suspicion of a plot led him to imprison and execute his minister Boethius.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hypatia
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician in Alexandria, lynched by a mob incited under Cyril's influence; her death, Russell notes, marked the end of philosophy at Alexandria.

core_concepts.name: The Nestorian controversy (two Persons vs. one)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A theological dispute over whether Christ was really two separate persons -- one human, one divine -- joined together, or a single, unified person.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Christological dispute, chiefly between Nestorius and Cyril, over whether Christ's divinity and humanity constitute two distinct Persons (Nestorius's view) or are united in a single Person, and, if united, whether in one nature or two.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It generated, in Russell's words, 'an almost incredible degree of passion and fury,' split the Eastern and Western Church along roughly the Suez line, and produced a lasting schism (Nestorianism) that spread across Syria, Persia, India, and China, weakening Byzantine control over Syria and facilitating the later Arab conquest.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Came to a head when Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, objected to calling the Virgin Mary 'Mother of God,' since (on his view) she was mother only of the human Person, not the divine Person.
examples: The Council of Ephesus (431), where Western bishops arrived first, locked the doors against late-comers, and condemned Nestorius under Cyril's presidency
competing_positions: Cyril's doctrine of the unity of Christ's person
The Monophysite view (one nature only), later condemned at Chalcedon
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Nestorianism became a major missionary church across Asia; the persecution of Nestorians by Constantinople contributed, in Russell's account, to disaffection that assisted the Muslim conquest of Syria.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological and ecclesiastical-political, decided by council votes and imperial and papal backing rather than philosophical argument alone.

core_concepts.name: The Monophysite controversy (one nature)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The opposite theological error to Nestorianism: the view that Christ has only a single (divine) nature rather than two distinct natures, human and divine, in one person.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, condemned as heretical at the Council of Chalcedon (451), that Christ possesses only one nature rather than two natures (human and divine) united in one Person, which the Chalcedonian formula affirmed as orthodox.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Egypt adopted Monophysitism almost to a man, and the heresy spread up the Nile into Abyssinia; like Nestorianism in Syria, it weakened Byzantine religious unity and, Russell notes, facilitated the later Arab conquest of Egypt.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerged at a synod at Ephesus in 449, after Cyril's death, which Pope Leo secured the overturning of at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
examples: Mussolini's later citation of Abyssinian Monophysite 'heresy' as a pretext for conquest, noted by Russell as a modern echo
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Remained the doctrine of the Egyptian (Coptic) and Ethiopian churches into the modern period.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological, with lasting political consequences for Byzantine control of Egypt and Abyssinia.

core_concepts.name: The privative theory of evil
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Boethius's idea that evil is not really a 'thing' in its own right, but simply a lack or absence of good -- the way darkness is not a substance but merely the absence of light.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that evil has no positive existence but is merely a privation (deficiency) of good; since God, who is the chiefest good, can do everything, and God cannot do evil, evil must be nothing, i.e., not a positive reality God fails or refuses to produce.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It lets Boethius reconcile divine omnipotence and perfect goodness with the existence of apparent evil, and grounds his further claim that the wicked, lacking real being, are in fact weak, while the virtuous, possessing the good, are truly powerful.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in the Consolation of Philosophy (524), in the Platonic metaphysical tradition of treating imperfection as a lack implying a perfect pattern.
examples: 'Can God do evil? No. Therefore evil is nothing, since God can do everything.'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Transmitted a broadly Platonic and Neoplatonic treatment of the problem of evil into medieval Christian philosophy.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Framed in explicitly theological terms (God's omnipotence and goodness) though argued in a Platonic philosophical idiom.

core_concepts.name: Blessedness identified with divinity (Boethius's pantheistic strand)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Boethius argues that true happiness (blessedness) and God are ultimately the same thing, so that a person who achieves real happiness has, in some sense, become divine.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, in the Consolation, that blessedness and God are both the 'chiefest good' and are therefore identical, so that 'men are made happy by the obtaining of divinity' and 'every one that is happy is a god,' though by nature there is only one God and others are gods only 'by participation.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell notes this passes close to pantheism, and 'should have shocked Christians, but for some reason did not' -- an example of how thoroughly Platonic, rather than distinctively Christian, Boethius's philosophical content is.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in the metaphysical portions of the Consolation of Philosophy.
examples: 'They who obtain divinity become gods. Wherefore every one that is happy is a god.'
competing_positions: Orthodox Christian insistence on a strict distinction between Creator and creature
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Helped make the Consolation a vehicle for transmitting Platonism into the Middle Ages, especially once later ages supposed (on the strength of theological works of doubtful authenticity attributed to him) that Boethius was securely orthodox.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Theological in vocabulary but philosophically Platonic in substance.

core_concepts.name: Boethius's philosophic calm amid an age of superstition
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Written by a man awaiting execution, the Consolation shows none of the era's obsession with sin or morbid superstition; instead it displays a serene, rational, almost Socratic composure.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The distinctive tone Russell identifies in the Consolation: 'perfect philosophic calm,' free of the superstition, sin-obsession, and 'excessive straining after the unattainable' typical of the age, more reminiscent of Plato than of Plotinus.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is what makes Boethius, in Russell's judgment, utterly exceptional for his era -- a man free from superstition and fanaticism unmatched, Russell says, in the two centuries before or the ten centuries after him, and not paralleled again until after Newton.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed by Russell partly to Boethius's Roman aristocratic background, which may have made freedom from superstition less exceptional than elsewhere, though its combination with deep learning and public-spiritedness was, Russell says, unique for the age.
examples: The concluding poem on cosmic love and order, which Russell quotes in full and compares to Pope's Essay on Man
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Contributed to the Consolation's enormous medieval popularity and its influence on Dante, who Russell notes was likely influenced by its alternation of verse and prose in the Vita Nuova.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Notable for its comparative absence of religious anxiety despite being written by a condemned man under a Christian government.

arguments.title: The privation argument: evil as nothing
premises: God is the chiefest good, and His substance consists in nothing else but goodness.
God is omnipotent: He can do everything.
arguments.conclusion: Evil is nothing -- it has no positive reality -- since an omnipotent God, who can do everything, is unable to do it; what appears as evil is therefore merely a lack or deficiency of good, not a positive thing in its own right.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as classic Platonic metaphysics applied to theology: imperfection, on this view, is always a lack implying the existence of a perfect pattern (the good), rather than a rival positive force, so 'evil' names an absence rather than a substance.
implications: Grounds Boethius's further claim that the wicked, lacking real being (the good), are actually weak, while the virtuous, possessing it, are truly powerful.
Transmits a broadly Neoplatonic solution to the problem of evil into later medieval Christian philosophy.

arguments.title: Virtue as strength, wickedness as weakness
premises: All people, good and wicked alike, desire the good.
Only the virtuous actually obtain the good they desire.
To fail to obtain what one desires is a form of weakness or impotence.
arguments.conclusion: Virtuous men are always truly powerful and bad men always truly weak, since only the virtuous succeed in attaining what everyone, in fact, is really seeking.
arguments.explanation: Boethius extends the privative theory of evil into ethics: since evil is a deficiency rather than a substance, the wicked, who fail to attain the good, are in a state of genuine lack or impotence, however outwardly successful they may appear; the wicked are worse off if they escape earthly punishment than if they suffer it, since punishment at least corrects the deficiency.
objections: Russell notes, in an aside, that this could not consistently be said of eternal punishment in hell.
implications: Supports the Consolation's larger argument that external fortune (wealth, power, reputation) is irrelevant to true happiness, which depends only on possessing the good.
Reinforces the work's overall tone of philosophic calm in the face of Boethius's own impending execution.

key_distinctions: Nestorius's 'two Persons' vs. the Monophysite 'one nature' vs. the Chalcedonian formula of 'two natures, one Person'
Positive being (the good) vs. privation/deficiency (evil), in Boethius's Platonic metaphysics
Boethius's purely Platonic philosophical content vs. his later medieval reputation as an orthodox Church Father
The era's general superstition and sin-obsession vs. Boethius's exceptional philosophic calm
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Boethius explicitly names Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle as the 'true philosophers,' dismissing Stoics and Epicureans as usurpers of the name, though Russell notes his ethical content draws heavily on Seneca and Stoic morality in practice. The Consolation's metaphysics -- the privative theory of evil, the identification of blessedness with divinity -- is, per Russell, purely Platonic, including a versified summary of the opening of the Timaeus. The Christological controversies of this chapter also involve the Neoplatonic intellectual world of Alexandria, symbolized by the murder of the Neoplatonist Hypatia.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell credits Boethius with transmitting Platonism into the medieval world under cover of an assumed orthodoxy secured by theological works (on the Trinity, among others) that many authorities consider spurious. He notes a resemblance between the Consolation's alternation of prose and verse and Dante's Vita Nuova, and remarks that one does not find a comparably serene, undogmatic philosophical outlook again until after Newton.
political_social_context: The chapter traces how Church councils were also political battles: the Council of Ephesus (431) was decided by the Western bishops' procedural maneuvering in Cyril's favor, and the Council of Chalcedon (451) was secured chiefly through the influence of Pope Leo. Christological schism weakened Byzantine control at the religious peripheries (Nestorian Syria, Monophysite Egypt and Abyssinia), which Russell links to the later ease of Arab conquest. Boethius's own political career -- consul, then chief minister to Theodoric -- ended in his imprisonment and execution on suspicion of conspiracy, occasioned by rising tension between the Arian Theodoric and his increasingly assertive Catholic subjects after Justin's proscription of Arianism in 523.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter surveys the violent Christological disputes of the fifth-century Church, the lynching of the philosopher Hypatia as a marker of philosophy's end in Alexandria, and Justinian's closing of the pagan schools of philosophy at Athens in 529, after which the dispossessed philosophers briefly sought refuge with the Persian king before returning home in obscurity.
russell_presentation: Russell treats the fifth century as philosophically barren -- 'there was little philosophy' after Augustine's death -- but historically consequential, and narrates the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies with open irony, describing the Council of Ephesus's 'episcopal tumult' as retrospectively acquiring 'the venerable aspect of the Third Œcumenical Council,' and drawing heavily and explicitly on Gibbon for the lynching of Hypatia. His tone shifts sharply for Boethius, whom he singles out as an extraordinary and admirable exception: a man of 'perfect philosophic calm' writing 'as admirable as the last moments of the Platonic Socrates' while awaiting execution, whose freedom from superstition and fanaticism Russell judges unmatched for twelve centuries either side of his life.
critical_context: Russell's account of Cyril, Hypatia, and the Council of Ephesus leans explicitly and heavily on Edward Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, which he quotes directly and cites by name; readers should note this is a documented historical source Russell is relying on and partly channeling, including its rhetorical color, rather than a fully independent assessment of the events.
key_takeaways: The fifth century, following Augustine's death, produced almost no original philosophy, being dominated instead by barbarian invasions and the collapse of the Western Empire.

The Nestorian controversy (two Persons vs. one) and the Monophysite controversy (one nature vs. two) convulsed the Church; Nestorius was condemned at Ephesus (431) and Monophysitism at Chalcedon (451), with both resulting schisms later weakening Byzantine control over Syria and Egypt.
Saint Cyril of Alexandria, though later venerated, is presented by Russell (via Gibbon) as a fanatic responsible for pogroms and for inciting the lynching of the Neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia.
Boethius, executed by Theodoric in 524, wrote the purely Platonic Consolation of Philosophy in prison; it was read throughout the Middle Ages as an orthodox Christian text despite its content.
Boethius's privative theory of evil holds that evil is not a positive reality but a mere deficiency of good, since an omnipotent, wholly good God cannot do evil.
Russell rates Boethius's philosophic calm in the face of execution as historically singular, unmatched, in his judgment, until after Newton.
study_notes:
This chapter works best read as two halves joined by a single theme: the near-total absence, and then sudden reappearance, of genuine philosophy in an age dominated by political collapse and theological faction. The first half -- barbarian invasions, then the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies -- shows what fills the vacuum when philosophical reasoning is displaced by dogmatic contest: councils decided by who locks the doors first, patriarchs canonized or condemned 'more or less by accident,' and mob violence against a philosopher (Hypatia) standing in for the end of philosophy itself at Alexandria. It is worth noticing that Russell treats these disputes as history and Church politics rather than as philosophy proper -- he gives them detailed narrative attention but does not credit either side with philosophical argument in the way he credits Augustine or Boethius.

The second half pivots sharply to Boethius, and the pivot is itself instructive: Russell is not simply cataloguing philosophers in sequence, but making a point about what real philosophy looks like by contrast with what preceded it in the chapter. Boethius's privative theory of evil and his identification of blessedness with divinity are Platonic doctrines, argued in a Platonic idiom, by a man who names Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle (not Christ or Scripture) as the 'true philosophers.' That the Middle Ages nonetheless read him as an orthodox Church authority -- helped along by theological works probably not his own -- is itself worth reflecting on: it shows how a rigorously philosophical text could be smuggled into the medieval canon under a label its actual content did not fully earn.

Finally, pay attention to the circumstances of composition. Russell repeatedly returns to the fact that the Consolation was written by a man awaiting execution, and treats this as raising the work's philosophical stakes rather than lowering them: the absence of fear, self-pity, or theological terror in the text is presented as evidence of a genuinely achieved philosophic detachment, not merely literary posturing.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The teaching, condemned as heretical, that Christ was two separate persons -- one human, one divine -- rather than a single unified person.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Christological position associated with Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus (431), which spread as a distinct church across Syria, Persia, India, and eventually China.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The teaching, also condemned as heretical, that Christ had only one nature rather than two (human and divine) joined in one person.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine that Christ possesses a single nature, condemned at the Council of Chalcedon (451) in favor of the formula of two natures united in one Person; adopted widely in Egypt and Abyssinia.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that evil is not a real 'thing' but simply the absence of good, the way darkness is the absence of light.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Boethius's Platonic doctrine that evil has no positive existence but is a privation (deficiency) of good, deduced from God's omnipotence and perfect goodness.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Boethius's book, written in prison while awaiting execution, in which the figure of Philosophy comforts him with arguments about true happiness, fortune, and the good.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A prosimetric (alternating prose and verse) philosophical dialogue composed by Boethius in 524, purely Platonic in metaphysical content though read throughout the Middle Ages as an orthodox Christian work.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Christian teaching, treated as heretical by the mainstream Church, that held Christ the Son was created by and subordinate to God the Father rather than co-eternal with Him.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Christological heresy denying the full co-equality of the Son with the Father; the creed of Theodoric and the Ostrogoths, whose tensions with Catholic Italy contributed to Boethius's downfall.

questions.prompt: What theological question was at the heart of the Nestorian controversy?
questions.answer: The relation of Christ's divinity to His humanity: whether there were two Persons (one human, one divine), as Nestorius held, or a single Person -- and if a single Person, whether one nature or two natures united in one Person.
questions.explanation: This dispute dominates the first part of the chapter and was decided against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus in 431.

questions.prompt: Which Roman senator, executed by Theodoric in 524, wrote the purely Platonic Consolation of Philosophy while in prison?
questions.explanation: Russell treats Boethius as the chapter's central philosophical figure, praising his work's serenity and Platonic rigor despite his impending execution.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what happened to the Neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia, and what does he say resulted from it?
questions.answer: She was dragged from her chariot, stripped, taken to a church, and killed by a mob incited under Cyril's influence, her flesh scraped off with oyster-shells; Russell states that after this, Alexandria was no longer troubled by philosophers.
questions.explanation: Russell presents her death, quoting Gibbon, as symbolically marking the end of philosophical life in Alexandria.

questions.prompt: Contrast the position of Nestorius with the Monophysite position condemned at Chalcedon.
questions.answer: Nestorius held that Christ's humanity and divinity constituted two separate Persons. The Monophysites, condemned at the opposite extreme, held that Christ had only one nature. The Council of Chalcedon (451) rejected both, affirming that Christ is one Person existing in two natures, human and divine.
questions.explanation: Russell presents these as the two opposed heresies bracketing the orthodox Chalcedonian formula.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Boethius's argument that evil is nothing.
questions.answer: God is the chiefest good, His substance consisting entirely in goodness; God is omnipotent, able to do everything; yet God cannot do evil; therefore evil must be nothing at all -- a mere absence of good rather than a positive reality -- since an omnipotent being's inability to do it shows it has no real being to be done.
questions.explanation: This is Boethius's privative theory of evil as Russell summarizes it from the Consolation of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, was Boethius's medieval reputation as an orthodox Christian author somewhat undeserved, based on the content of the Consolation itself?
questions.answer: Because the Consolation's philosophy is purely Platonic, naming Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle as the 'true philosophers,' and containing metaphysics (such as the identification of blessedness with divinity) that verges on pantheism; his orthodox reputation likely rested more on theological works, of doubtful authenticity, attributed to him.
questions.explanation: Russell stresses this gap between the Consolation's actual philosophical content and its medieval reception as an orthodox work.

quiz.prompt: Who wrote the Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution in 524?
quiz.explanation: Boethius, a Roman senator and minister to Theodoric, wrote the work in prison shortly before his execution.
quiz.related_concept: Boethius's philosophic calm amid an age of superstition

quiz.prompt: What did Nestorius hold about Christ's human and divine natures?
options: That they were a single nature
That they constituted two separate Persons
That only the divine nature existed
quiz.explanation: Nestorius held that Christ's humanity and divinity constituted two distinct Persons, which led him to object to calling Mary 'Mother of God.'
quiz.related_concept: The Nestorian controversy (two Persons vs. one)

quiz.prompt: The Council of Chalcedon (451) upheld the Monophysite doctrine that Christ has only one nature.
quiz.explanation: Chalcedon condemned Monophysitism, affirming instead that Christ exists in two natures, human and divine, united in one Person.

quiz.prompt: According to Boethius's privative theory, what is evil?
options: A positive substance created by Satan
A deficiency or absence of good, not a positive reality
An illusion with no relation to good or God
A necessary balance to goodness in the universe
quiz.explanation: Since God, the chiefest good, is omnipotent yet cannot do evil, Boethius concludes evil is nothing -- a mere privation of good.

quiz.prompt: Which philosopher was lynched by a mob in Alexandria, an event Russell treats as marking the end of philosophy there?
quiz.explanation: Hypatia, a Neoplatonist and mathematician, was killed by a mob incited under Cyril's influence.
quiz.related_concept: The Nestorian controversy (two Persons vs. one)

quiz.prompt: Boethius names Socrates, Plato, and ______ as the 'true philosophers,' dismissing the Stoics and Epicureans as usurpers of philosophy's name.
quiz.explanation: The Consolation opens by naming Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle as the genuine philosophers.
quiz.related_concept: Boethius's philosophic calm amid an age of superstition

quiz.prompt: Why does Russell say the Middle Ages regarded Boethius as an orthodox Christian, despite the Consolation's content being purely Platonic?
options: Because he explicitly renounced Platonism on his deathbed
Because of theological works, of doubtful authenticity, attributed to him, such as one on the Trinity
Because the Consolation quotes the Gospels extensively
Because he was canonized immediately after his death
quiz.explanation: Russell states it was probably owing to spuriously attributed theological works that the Middle Ages regarded Boethius as orthodox and drew on his Platonism without suspicion.
quiz.related_concept: Blessedness identified with divinity (Boethius's pantheistic strand)

quiz.prompt: What event does Russell say directly precipitated Boethius's imprisonment and execution?
options: His refusal to convert to Arianism
Theodoric's suspicion of a plot, following the Emperor Justin's proscription of Arianism in 523
His authorship of a treatise against the Trinity
A dispute with Pope Leo over the Council of Chalcedon
quiz.explanation: After Justin proscribed Arianism, the Arian Theodoric grew suspicious of Catholic Italy's loyalties and, believing there was a plot, imprisoned and executed his minister Boethius.
quiz.related_concept: Boethius's philosophic calm amid an age of superstition

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their role: (1) Cyril, (2) Nestorius, (3) Theodoric, (4) Justinian -- with (A) Ostrogothic king who executed Boethius, (B) patriarch who incited persecution of Jews and was linked to Hypatia's death, (C) closed the pagan schools of philosophy at Athens, (D) patriarch condemned as a heretic at Ephesus.
quiz.explanation: Cyril (B) incited persecution; Nestorius (D) was condemned at Ephesus; Theodoric (A) executed Boethius; Justinian (C) closed the Athenian schools.

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell narrates the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies with open irony, contrasting them sharply with his admiring treatment of Boethius. Analyze how Russell's tone and evaluative framing differ between these two parts of the chapter, and what this suggests about what he considers genuine philosophy versus theological faction.
rubric: Accurately summarizes the Christological controversies and Russell's ironic treatment of them
Accurately summarizes Boethius's Consolation and Russell's admiring treatment of it
